Project Python Foundations: FoodHub Data Analysis¶

Context¶

The number of restaurants in New York is increasing day by day. Lots of students and busy professionals rely on those restaurants due to their hectic lifestyles. Online food delivery service is a great option for them. It provides them with good food from their favorite restaurants. A food aggregator company FoodHub offers access to multiple restaurants through a single smartphone app.

The app allows the restaurants to receive a direct online order from a customer. The app assigns a delivery person from the company to pick up the order after it is confirmed by the restaurant. The delivery person then uses the map to reach the restaurant and waits for the food package. Once the food package is handed over to the delivery person, he/she confirms the pick-up in the app and travels to the customer's location to deliver the food. The delivery person confirms the drop-off in the app after delivering the food package to the customer. The customer can rate the order in the app. The food aggregator earns money by collecting a fixed margin of the delivery order from the restaurants.

Objective¶

The food aggregator company has stored the data of the different orders made by the registered customers in their online portal. They want to analyze the data to get a fair idea about the demand of different restaurants which will help them in enhancing their customer experience. Suppose you are hired as a Data Scientist in this company and the Data Science team has shared some of the key questions that need to be answered. Perform the data analysis to find answers to these questions that will help the company to improve the business.

Data Description¶

The data contains the different data related to a food order. The detailed data dictionary is given below.

Data Dictionary¶

  • order_id: Unique ID of the order
  • customer_id: ID of the customer who ordered the food
  • restaurant_name: Name of the restaurant
  • cuisine_type: Cuisine ordered by the customer
  • cost_of_the_order: Cost of the order
  • day_of_the_week: Indicates whether the order is placed on a weekday or weekend (The weekday is from Monday to Friday and the weekend is Saturday and Sunday)
  • rating: Rating given by the customer out of 5
  • food_preparation_time: Time (in minutes) taken by the restaurant to prepare the food. This is calculated by taking the difference between the timestamps of the restaurant's order confirmation and the delivery person's pick-up confirmation.
  • delivery_time: Time (in minutes) taken by the delivery person to deliver the food package. This is calculated by taking the difference between the timestamps of the delivery person's pick-up confirmation and drop-off information

Observations:¶
  • The mean cost of the orders is 16.499 dollar, and the median is slightly lower at 14.140 dollar, indicating a slight right skew.
  • The distribution shows a multimodal data.
  • There is a reasonable spread in the data, with most orders clustered around 12 to 23 dollar.
  • The box plot doesn't show any outliers.
  • The distribution is right-skewed, meaning there are more low-cost orders than high-cost ones.

    • The box plot doesn't show any outliers.
    • There is a reasonable spread in the data, with most orders clustered around 23 to 31 minutes.

Question 9: What percentage of the orders cost more than 20 dollars? [2 marks]¶

In [78]:
# First we find the number of orders more than 20
condition = df['cost_of_the_order'] > 20
number_of_orders_more_than_20 = len(df[condition])
print('Number of orders that cost more than 20 dollars: ',number_of_orders_more_than_20)

# Now the number of all orders
number_of_all_orders = len(df)
print('Number of all orders: ',number_of_all_orders)

# Finally, the percentage of the orders more than 20
percentage_of_orders_more_than_20 = (number_of_orders_more_than_20 / number_of_all_orders) * 100
print(f'Percentage of the orders cost more than 20 dollars: {round(percentage_of_orders_more_than_20,2)}%')

Find the restaurants fulfilling the criteria to get the promotional offer. [3 marks]¶

# Copy the data and convert rating from string to number
df_promo = df.copy()
df_promo['rating'] = pd.to_numeric(df_promo['rating'], errors='coerce')

# Group the resturand and apply count and mean function on the rating to have a new dataframe
restaurant_ratings = df_promo.groupby('restaurant_name')['rating'].agg(['count', 'mean'])

# apply conditions
promotional_restaurants = restaurant_ratings[(restaurant_ratings['count'] > 50) & (restaurant_ratings['mean'] > 4)]

print(promotional_restaurants)

Question 14: The company charges the restaurant 25% on the orders having cost greater than 20 dollars and 15% on the orders having cost greater than 5 dollars. Find the net revenue generated by the company across all orders. [3 marks]¶

In [96]:
# Find the order costs more than 20 and apply the charge on sum of them
revenue_upper_20 = df[df['cost_of_the_order'] > 20]['cost_of_the_order'].sum() * 0.25

# Find the order costs betweeen 5 and 20 apply the charge on sum of them
df_less_20 = df[df['cost_of_the_order'] <= 20]
df_less_20_upper_5 = df_less_20[df_less_20['cost_of_the_order'] > 5]
revenue_5 = df_less_20_upper_5['cost_of_the_order'].sum() * 0.15

# Calculate the total revenue
total_revenue = revenue_upper_20 + revenue_5

print('The net revenue generated by the company across all orders is: ',total_revenue)

Conclusion and Recommendations¶

Question 17: What are your conclusions from the analysis? What recommendations would you like to share to help improve the business? (You can use cuisine type and feedback ratings to drive your business recommendations.) [6 marks]¶

Conclusions:¶

Ratings

  • Lack of Clear Pattern: There is no clear pattern between users and the ratings they give. The only notable observation is that the ratings are above 3, suggesting that users may choose not to rate foods they did not enjoy.
  • Missing Ratings in Certain Cuisines: Some types of cuisine have a high number of missing ratings.
  • Restaurants Without Ratings: There are restaurants that do not have any ratings at all, and the number of orders for them is low.
  • Order Cost vs. Ratings: Higher-rated orders (ratings 4 and 5) tend to have a wide range of order costs, but there is no strong indication that cost directly influences ratings. Orders with lower ratings are spread across various cost ranges, indicating that other factors likely play a significant role in customer satisfaction.

Cuisine Type

  • Most Popular Cuisine: The most popular cuisine is American food.
  • Cuisine Type and Preparation Time: There is no relationship between cuisine type and food preparation time.

Delivery and Preparation Time

  • Correlation Between Preparation and Delivery Times: There is a correlation between preparation and delivery times. Addressing bottlenecks to reduce high preparation times could lead to faster deliveries, enhancing customer satisfaction.

  • Weekend Variability: Delivery times appear to be slightly more varied on weekends. This might suggest higher demand or traffic-related delays on weekends.

Order Volume Variations

  • Variation Across Weekdays and Weekends: There is variation in order volume across weekdays and weekends, with busier days affecting order flow.

Insights into “Not Given” Ratings

  • Restaurants with High “Not Given” Ratings:

Certain restaurants, such as Shake Shack, The Meatball Shop, and Blue Ribbon Sushi, have significantly higher counts of “Not given” ratings. These restaurants may benefit from targeted efforts to encourage feedback, perhaps through incentives or follow-up reminders.

  • Cuisine Types with High “Not Given” Ratings:

American, Japanese, and Italian cuisines have the most “Not given” ratings, suggesting a possible trend among customers ordering these cuisines to skip feedback. Highlighting the importance of reviews for these cuisine types could improve engagement.

  • Customers Frequently Giving “Not Given” Ratings:

A few customers appear to consistently leave “Not given” ratings. Identifying these customers and possibly offering loyalty rewards or feedback incentives could encourage them to participate more actively in rating.

Recommendations:¶

  1. Enhance Customer Feedback:

    Encourage customers to provide ratings, as a large portion of orders lacks feedback. This information could guide targeted improvements.

  2. Incentivize Feedback for Certain Restaurants and Cuisines:

    Target restaurants with higher “Not given” ratings by offering discounts or loyalty points for reviews to enhance engagement.

  3. Create Feedback Incentives for Repeat Non-Raters:

    Implement a reward system for customers who consistently provide ratings, especially those who typically skip feedback, to encourage more consistent reviews.

  4. Improve Feedback Request Timing:

    Test different timings for feedback requests, such as sending reminders a few hours after delivery for popular cuisines or top restaurants, to capture more customer experiences.

  5. Optimize Weekend Operations:

    Given the variance in delivery times on weekends, focusing on efficiency or managing order capacity on these days could enhance the customer experience.

  6. Cuisine-Based Promotions:

    Popular cuisines could be highlighted in promotions, and targeted discounts or loyalty incentives could help drive up order frequency for less popular cuisines.

  7. Focus on Cuisine Types with Higher Variability in Ratings:

    Some cuisine types show mixed ratings. Focusing on these areas to improve consistency can enhance customer satisfaction.

  8. Improve Efficiency in Delivery and Preparation:

    Addressing bottlenecks to reduce high preparation times could lead to faster deliveries, enhancing customer satisfaction.

  9. Highlight Popular Cuisines on Key Days:

    Given the variation in order volume across weekdays and weekends, promote popular cuisines on busier days to optimize order flow and ensure high customer engagement during peak times.
